questions.prompt: A planar 2-link arm has link lengths 0.5 m and 0.3 m and no joint limits. The reachable workspace is a ring (annulus). What is the inner radius of that ring, in meters?
questions.explanation: The inner radius is the difference of the link lengths: |0.5 − 0.3| = 0.2 m (the outer radius is the sum, 0.8 m).

questions.prompt: For a given target end-effector pose, inverse kinematics can have zero, exactly one, or many solutions.
questions.explanation: A target outside the workspace has no solution, while different joint configurations can reach the same pose.

questions.prompt: How many degrees of freedom does a rigid body confined to a flat plane have?
questions.explanation: Two numbers give position (x, y) and one gives orientation (θ), so 3. A free body in 3D has 6.

questions.prompt: A wheel with circumference 0.25 m has an encoder of 1440 ticks per revolution. The encoder counts 2160 ticks. How far did the wheel travel, in meters?
Which of these are proprioceptive sensors (they measure the robot's own internal state)?
questions.explanation: LIDAR and cameras measure the external world, so they are exteroceptive.

questions.prompt: Match each sensing idea to its description.
pairs: Wheel encoder
Counts ticks to estimate the robot's own motion
LIDAR
Times a laser pulse's return to measure distance
Camera
Grid of pixels with no direct distance information
Sensor fusion
Combines complementary sensors for a better estimate
questions.explanation: Each description is the defining characteristic of that sensing approach.

questions.prompt: Dead-reckoning errors tend to average out over time, so position estimates get more accurate the longer the robot drives.
questions.explanation: Each step's error is built into the next estimate, so errors accumulate as drift rather than canceling.

questions.prompt: What does a loop closure give a SLAM system?
choices: A recognized return to a previously mapped place, which lets drift in the whole path be corrected
A map without needing any sensors
A guarantee that no obstacles are present
questions.answer: A recognized return to a previously mapped place, which lets drift in the whole path be corrected
questions.explanation: Recognizing a revisit shows the accumulated estimate is wrong, so the path and map can be adjusted consistently.

questions.prompt: What is the name for estimating position by accumulating small measured motions from a known starting pose, without external landmarks? (two words)
questions.explanation: Dead reckoning adds up measured motions; its wheel-encoder version is called odometry.

questions.prompt: In A* search a node has actual cost from the start g(n) = 12 and heuristic estimate to the goal h(n) = 5. What is f(n)?
Put the stages of a robot's path planning workflow in order.
items: Inflate the map's obstacles by the robot's size (configuration space)
Turn the free cells of the inflated map into graph nodes and edges
Search the graph for a global path with A*
Adjust locally around newly seen obstacles while driving
Replan if the route becomes blocked
questions.explanation: Obstacles are inflated so the robot can be treated as a point, the free space becomes a graph, A* searches it globally, and surprises are handled locally first and by replanning when the route is blocked.

questions.prompt: Why must A*'s heuristic never overestimate the true remaining cost?
choices: So that A* is guaranteed to find the lowest-cost path
So that the graph has fewer nodes
So that the robot moves more slowly
So that obstacles are inflated correctly
questions.answer: So that A* is guaranteed to find the lowest-cost path
questions.explanation: An admissible heuristic (one that never overestimates) keeps A* from skipping the true best route.

questions.prompt: A path from A* already includes timing information telling the robot when to be at each point.
questions.explanation: A path is only a sequence of positions; a trajectory adds timing, respecting velocity and acceleration limits.

questions.prompt: Explain why pure pursuit aims at a lookahead point on the path instead of the very next waypoint, and why feedback control is still needed on top of it.
rubric: Says aiming at the next waypoint causes sharp corner cutting or oscillation
Says the lookahead point moves along the path ahead of the robot, giving smoother steering
Says pure pursuit steers from path geometry and does not correct for tracking error by itself
Says feedback compares actual pose to intended pose and commands a correction
questions.model: Steering straight at the next waypoint makes small position errors cause abrupt steering changes, which can cause oscillation. Pure pursuit instead chases a point a fixed distance ahead on the path, which gives smoother steering. It still needs feedback control because it only follows the path geometry; feedback measures the difference between the actual and intended pose and commands a correction to close the gap.
questions.explanation: Lookahead smooths steering, and feedback keeps the robot on the timed trajectory.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the steering strategy that continuously aims at a point a fixed lookahead distance ahead on the path? (two words)
questions.explanation: Pure pursuit chases a moving lookahead point along the path.

questions.prompt: A behavior tree Sequence has children [Attempt Grasp, Verify Grasp]. If Attempt Grasp returns Failure, what happens?
choices: The Sequence fails immediately without running Verify Grasp
The tree restarts from the leaf
questions.answer: The Sequence fails immediately without running Verify Grasp
questions.explanation: A Sequence succeeds only if all children succeed and stops at the first failure.

questions.prompt: Match each control concept to its description.
pairs: Reactive control
Maps sensed conditions directly to actions with little lookahead
Deliberative control
Builds and reasons over a model before acting
Finite state machine
A fixed set of states with condition-triggered transitions
Behavior tree
A tree of nodes returning Success, Failure, or Running
questions.explanation: Each is a standard way to structure a robot's decision-making.

questions.prompt: A Selector (fallback) node in a behavior tree succeeds as soon as any one of its children succeeds.
questions.explanation: A Selector tries children in order and only fails if all of them fail.

questions.prompt: Each of two gripper fingers presses on an object with a normal force of 20 N, and the friction coefficient is μ = 0.5 at each contact. What is the maximum total friction force available from both contacts before slipping, in newtons?
questions.explanation: Each contact gives μN = 0.5 × 20 = 10 N, so the two contacts together give 20 N.

questions.prompt: Put the stages of a manipulation pipeline in order.
items: Perceive the object and its pose
Plan a grasp and a reachable approach
Grasp by closing the gripper with appropriate force
Place the object and release it
questions.explanation: The pipeline is Perceive, Plan, Grasp, Place, and each stage depends on the one before.

questions.prompt: Which end-effector is suited to picking up a flat, thin sheet that a rigid two-finger gripper cannot get fingers around?
questions.explanation: A suction cup holds a surface by pressure difference and needs no opposing surfaces or finger clearance.

questions.prompt: Match each case study (or failure type) from this unit to its distinguishing feature.
pairs: Warehouse robots
Floor fiducial markers as low-drift landmarks
Robot vacuums
Camera-based SLAM combined with wheel odometry
Self-driving vehicles
Perception demands far higher in speed and stakes
Seam failure
Two correct components make incompatible assumptions about each other
questions.explanation: Each item summarizes a point from the case studies and failure-mode lessons.

questions.prompt: A seam failure can occur even when every individual component works exactly as designed in isolation.
questions.explanation: Seam failures come from incompatible assumptions at the boundaries between components, not from a broken component.

questions.prompt: Describe one example of a seam failure between two parts of an autonomy stack and explain how you would catch it.
rubric: Names two components of the stack that each work in isolation
States the incompatible assumption between them
Explains the wrong or unsafe combined behavior
Proposes testing the integrated system rather than only unit-testing each part
questions.model: For example, a planner may assume the robot can turn in place, while the motion controller assumes a minimum turning radius. Each is correct alone, but together the robot cannot follow the planned path. Testing each part in isolation will not reveal this, so the integrated system must be tested end to end and the assumptions between layers made explicit.
questions.explanation: Seam failures only appear when components are tested together.
